preamble: De-affrication of [ts] to [s] is a common historical development in which the stop onset of the affricate is lost, leaving only the sibilant fricative. It occurred in Old French (centum > [tsent] > [sɑ̃]), in 16th-century Spanish (where /ts/ deaffricated to [s̪] by 1600 before becoming Castilian /θ/ or merging with /s/ under seseo), and in prehistoric Greek, where *ts from palatalized *ky, *khy and *ty yielded Ionic ss (later simplified to [s] in Modern Greek).

examples.note: Latin centum evolved into Old French [tsent], which subsequently de-affricated to [s] in Middle and Modern French.
By 1600 the affricate /ts/ (spelled c before e/i and ç) had deaffricated to dental [s̪]; in Andalusian, Canarian and American seseo it merged with /s/, so 'ciento' sounds like 'siento' 'I feel'.
Pre-Greek *ts arising from palatalization became Ionic σσ /sː/ (Attic ττ); similarly *tag-yō > *tatsō > τάσσω 'I arrange'. Modern Greek simplified the geminate to [s].

Sihler, A. L. (1995). New Comparative Grammar of Greek and Latin. Oxford University Press. https://academic.oup.com/book/47067
Campbell, L. (2013). Historical Linguistics: An Introduction (3rd ed.). Edinburgh University Press.
